name: Pericles
info: Pericles (c. 495–429 BCE) was an Athenian statesman and general who led Athens from about 461 BCE until his death, turned the Delian League into an Athenian empire and began the building programme of the Acropolis.

facts.born: c. 495 BCE in Athens; son of the politician Xanthippus and of Agariste, of the noble family of the Alcmaeonidae
facts.died: 429 BCE in Athens, of the plague that struck the city early in the Peloponnesian War
facts.role: Athenian statesman and orator; leader of the democratic party from about 461 BCE; strategos (general), re-elected yearly, the only office he officially held; deposed and fined in 430 BCE and re-elected in 429 BCE
facts.known: the "Age of Pericles" in Athens; the building programme of the Acropolis, including the Parthenon; turning the Delian League into an Athenian empire; the citizenship law of 451 BCE; the defensive strategy of the first years of the Peloponnesian War; the Funeral Oration as Thucydides gives it

t: Born into the Alcmaeonid family through his mother, Pericles rose with the democratic party, saw his rival Cimon ostracised in 461 BCE, and led Athens until he died in 429 BCE.

He paid citizens for jury service, restricted citizenship to children of two Athenian parents, and drew on the treasury of the Delian League to fund the temples of the Acropolis, a use of the allies' money one modern scholar has called one of the largest embezzlements in history.
His defensive strategy in the Peloponnesian War, and his part in bringing the war about, have divided historians from Plutarch and Thucydides to Donald Kagan and Victor Davis Hanson.
dyk: Contemporary comedians mocked the unusually large size of Pericles's skull, calling him "Squill-head" after the sea-onion; Plutarch claimed this was why he was always shown in a helmet, but the helmet was the symbol of his rank as general.
ev: Born in Athens, the son of Xanthippus and of Agariste of the Alcmaeonidae
Pays for the staging of Aeschylus's The Persians at the Greater Dionysia, a sign of his wealth
After Ephialtes's reform of the Areopagus, secures the ostracism of his rival Cimon
Proposes the law limiting Athenian citizenship to those of Athenian parentage on both sides
Proposes a decree allowing 9,000 talents to be used for rebuilding the temples of Athens
Leads the expedition against Samos, which capitulates after a siege of eight months
As Sparta invades, brings the people of Attica within the walls of Athens, and that winter delivers the Funeral Oration
Re-elected strategos a year after being deposed and fined, he dies of the plague, which had killed both his legitimate sons

sections.early:
Pericles was born around 495 BCE in Athens, the son of the politician Xanthippus and of Agariste, a member of the powerful and controversial noble family of the Alcmaeonidae. Xanthippus was ostracised in 485–484 BCE but returned to command the Athenian contingent at the Greek victory at Mycale five years later. Agariste was the great-granddaughter of Cleisthenes, tyrant of Sicyon, and the niece of the Athenian reformer Cleisthenes, and her family's connections helped to start her son's political career. He belonged to the Attic phyle of Acamantis.

According to Herodotus and Plutarch, Agariste dreamed a few nights before his birth that she had borne a lion. The story may allude to the unusually large size of his skull, a favourite target of the comedians. His early years were quiet: the introverted young man avoided public appearances and gave his time to study, which his family's nobility and wealth allowed. He learned music from the masters of the time, perhaps Damon or Pythocleides, and he is considered the first politician to attribute importance to philosophy. He kept company with Protagoras, Zeno of Elea and Anaxagoras, who became a close friend. His proverbial calm and self-control, and perhaps his manner of thought and speech, are often regarded as products of Anaxagoras's influence.
sections.rise:
In the spring of 472 BCE Pericles paid for the staging of Aeschylus's The Persians at the Greater Dionysia, a liturgy that showed him to be one of the wealthier men of Athens; Simon Hornblower has argued that the choice of a play recalling Themistocles's victory at Salamis signalled support for Themistocles against Cimon. Plutarch says that Pericles stood first among the Athenians for forty years, which would place his leadership from the early 460s BCE. In 463 BCE he was the leading prosecutor of Cimon, leader of the conservative faction, who was acquitted.

Around 461 BCE Ephialtes, leader of the democratic party and Pericles's mentor, proposed cutting the powers of the Areopagus, the aristocratic council, and the Assembly adopted the proposal without opposition. In the same year Pericles achieved the ostracism of Cimon, accused of betraying the city by aiding Sparta, and the murder of Ephialtes left him free to consolidate his authority. He promoted a populist social policy: free theatre seats for the poor, a lower property requirement for the archonship in 458–457 BCE and wages for jurymen soon after 454 BCE. In 444 BCE the new conservative leader Thucydides (not the historian) accused him of profligacy over the building plan; Pericles offered to repay the questioned costs himself if the dedications bore his name, and in 442 BCE Thucydides was ostracised for ten years.
sections.deeds:
After 442 BCE Pericles was re-elected every year to the generalship, the only office he ever officially held, though his influence made him the de facto ruler of the state. He completed the transformation of the Delian League into an Athenian empire. The league's treasury was moved from Delos to Athens in 454–453 BCE, revolts in Miletus and Erythrae were put down by 450–449 BCE, and around 447 BCE the Coinage Decree imposed Athenian silver coinage, weights and measures on the allies. From that treasury came the funds for the building plan of the Acropolis, including the Propylaea, the Parthenon and the golden statue of Athena by his friend Phidias; in 449 BCE he proposed a decree allowing 9,000 talents to be spent on the temples.

His campaigns brought both gains and losses. In 447 BCE he settled Athenian colonists in the Gallipoli peninsula, but after the defeat at Coronea Athens lost Boeotia. When Euboea revolted in 446 BCE he crushed the rising: the landowners of Chalcis lost their properties, and the people of Histiaea, who had killed the crew of an Athenian trireme, were uprooted and replaced by 2,000 Athenian settlers. The Thirty Years' Peace of 446–445 BCE gave up most of Athens's gains on the mainland. In 440 BCE he led the war against Samos, which surrendered after a siege of eight months, and he founded cleruchies at Andros, Naxos, Thurii and Amphipolis.
sections.opponents:
Pericles was attacked throughout his career. His conservative opponents charged him with squandering public money, and just before the Peloponnesian War his closest associates were prosecuted: Phidias for embezzling gold meant for the statue of Athena and then for impiety, Anaxagoras for his religious beliefs, and his companion Aspasia of Miletus of corrupting the women of Athens, charges that were probably nothing more than unproven slanders. Aspasia was acquitted after a rare emotional outburst from Pericles; according to Plutarch, Phidias died in prison, though this is debated. Pericles himself was asked to account for his handling of public funds.

Critics since have judged his measures harshly. Plato has Socrates say that Pericles made the Athenians "slothful, garrulous and avaricious" by starting the system of public fees, and Plutarch reports others who blamed him for leading the people into bad habits. The 19th-century historian Constantine Paparrigopoulos held that his populism led to the political turmoil after his death, and the Greek academician Angelos Vlachos called his use of the allies' treasury one of the largest embezzlements in human history. Plutarch suggests that he and the Athenians incited the war, and Karl Julius Beloch believes he brought it on to protect his position at home. Of his strategy, Donald Kagan called it "a form of wishful thinking that failed", and Barry S. Strauss and Josiah Ober judged that as a strategist he was a failure.
sections.last:
Pericles held that war with Sparta was inevitable. He sent help to Corcyra against Corinth and proposed the Megarian decree, which shut Megarian merchants out of the markets of Athens and the ports of its empire; George Cawkwell argues that it breached the Thirty Years' Peace. Sparta demanded, among other things, the expulsion of the Alcmaeonidae, Pericles included, and in a speech Thucydides gives him he urged the Athenians not to yield. When Archidamus II invaded Attica in 431 BCE, Pericles had already moved the whole population of the countryside within the walls of Athens, refused battle and sent a fleet of 100 ships to raid the Peloponnese. In the winter of 431–430 BCE he delivered the Funeral Oration for the city's dead.

In the summer of 430 BCE an epidemic devastated the crowded city. Public anger turned on Pericles: he was deprived of the generalship and fined between 15 and 50 talents, with Cleon named as prosecutor in the ancient sources. Within a year the Athenians re-elected him, but in 429 BCE the plague killed his sister and his two legitimate sons, Paralus and Xanthippus. The Athenians then made his son by Aspasia, Pericles the Younger, a citizen, though his own law of 451 BCE barred him. Pericles died of the plague later that year. On his deathbed, Plutarch reports, he said that "no living Athenian ever put on mourning because of me". Thucydides judged his death a disaster for Athens.
sections.legacy:
The most visible legacy of Pericles is the art and literature of the Golden Age, much of which survives; the Acropolis, though in ruins, is a symbol of modern Athens. The years from about 461 to 429 BCE are sometimes called the "Age of Pericles", and it was principally through his efforts that Athens gained its reputation as the educational and cultural centre of the Greek world. He has been lauded as "the ideal type of the perfect statesman in ancient Greece", and his Funeral Oration is now synonymous with participatory democracy and civic pride. Victor L. Ehrenberg, by contrast, argues that a basic element of his legacy is an Athenian imperialism that denied democracy and freedom to all but the ruling state.

How much of his voice survives is uncertain. Pericles never wrote down his speeches, and Thucydides recreated three of them, so scholars such as Ioannis Kakridis and Arnold Gomme have debated how far the words are Thucydides's own. Thucydides, an admirer, wrote that Athens was "in name a democracy but, in fact, governed by its first citizen". His war strategy still divides historians: Hans Delbrück called him one of the greatest statesmen and military leaders in history, Athanasios Platias and Constantinos Koliopoulos argue that Athens lost only when it abandoned his strategy, and others hold that it was too defensive to succeed.

summary: Pericles led Athens as its foremost orator and general from about 461 to 429 BCE, widening its democracy, turning the Delian League into an empire and funding the Parthenon from the allies' treasury. He took Athens into the Peloponnesian War and died of the plague in its third year, leaving a record that historians have praised and condemned ever since.
